Part 5A Worked Solutions: the Supplied ‘Exercise 2 – Carbocation Stability Order’ (redrawn)

These are the stability-order problems you supplied (Exercise 2, Q1–Q35, and two multiple-choice questions). The structures are redrawn here from the images and the reasoning is new. Each answer is the order of decreasing stability, using the standard JEE-Advanced conventions: stability rises with substitution, resonance donors (+M), hyperconjugation (number and quality of C–H/C–C bonds in the correct position), aromaticity; falls with −I/−M groups, antiaromaticity and bridgehead (non-planar) geometry. For isotopes: C–H hyperconjugation > C–D > C–T when the isotopic group is on the carbon next to the cationic centre, but only the +I order (T > D > H) operates when the group is further away. Items I could not read with certainty (Q4, Q18, Q19, Q22, Q33, Q34) are listed at the end for you to confirm.

E2-1.
Arrange 1–3 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 3 > 2 > 1
Tertiary > secondary > primary: the number of alkyl groups on the cationic carbon (hyperconjugation and +I).
E2-2.
Arrange 1–3 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 1 > 3 > 2
1 is tertiary, 3 secondary, 2 primary (the 2-methylbutyl cation would rearrange, but as drawn it is primary).
E2-3.
Arrange 1–3 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 1 > 2 > 3
1 is tertiary. 2 and 3 are secondary; the methyl group is adjacent to the cationic carbon in 2 (its C–H and C–C bonds hyperconjugate/β-branching), but only γ in 3 (+I only).
E2-5.
Arrange 1–3 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 1 > 2 > 3
1 is tertiary. 2 and 3 are secondary; 2 has the more alkyl-branched neighbourhood (a quaternary carbon next to C+), 3 only a remote methyl.
E2-6.
Arrange 1–3 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 3 > 2 > 1
The labelled methyl groups are on the carbon next to the quaternary carbon, i.e. γ to C+: no C–H/C–D/C–T bond is hyperconjugating. Only the inductive effect operates, and D and T are slightly more electron-releasing than H (T > D > H).
E2-7.
Arrange 1–3 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 1 > 2 > 3
Now the labelled group is directly on C+: hyperconjugation σ(C–X) → p operates, and C–H is a better donor than C–D, which is better than C–T (lower zero-point energy, shorter amplitude for the heavier isotope). β-Deuterium slows ionisation by about 1.3–2 per CD3.
E2-8.
Arrange 1–3 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 3 > 2 > 1
A meta substituent cannot hyperconjugate with the benzylic cation (no resonance contributor puts charge on the meta carbon), so only the +I effect counts: CT3 > CD3 > CH3.
E2-9.
Arrange 1–3 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 1 > 2 > 3
m-CH3 is weakly +I, m-CN and m-NO2 are −I (σm 0.56 and 0.71): the stronger the −I, the less stable the cation.
E2-10.
Arrange 1–3 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 1 > 2 > 3
p-Alkyl groups stabilise by hyperconjugation (charge is on the para carbon): C–H > C–D > C–T.
E2-11.
Arrange 1–3 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 1 > 2 > 3
p-CH3 donates; p-CN and p-NO2 withdraw by −I and −M (σ+ 0.66 and 0.79), NO2 more strongly.
E2-12.
Arrange 1–3 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 1 > 3 > 2
Baker–Nathan order in solution: the number of hyperconjugating α-C–H bonds on the ring carbon: CH3 (3) > CH2R (2) > CHR2 (1). (In the gas phase the order reverses, because polarisability then dominates.)
E2-13.
Arrange 1–3 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 2 > 3 > 1
All are benzylic; each α-methyl group adds hyperconjugation/+I: tertiary (cumyl) > secondary (1-phenylethyl) > primary (benzyl).
E2-14.
Arrange 1–3 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 3 > 2 > 1
No substituent is best. A meta halogen is only −I (no +M can reach the benzylic cation from the meta position), and Cl is more electronegative than Br (σm+ 0.40 vs 0.41, nearly equal; the conventional answer is Cl more destabilising).
E2-15.
Arrange 1–3 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 1 > 2 > 3
p-NH2 and p-OH are +M donors (the quinoid iminium/oxocarbenium contributor); nitrogen is the better donor (σ+ −1.3 vs −0.92).
E2-16.
Arrange 1–3 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 3 > 2 > 1
Each additional phenyl delocalises the charge further: trityl (pKR+ −6.6) > diphenylmethyl (−13.3) > benzyl.
E2-17.
Arrange 1–3 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 1 > 2 > 3
A cyclopropyl ring on the benzene ring donates through its bent bonds (σ+ −0.41); each extra methyl on the ring adds +I/hyperconjugation to the donor.
E2-20.
Arrange 1–3 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 3 > 2 > 1
Each cyclopropyl group donates its bent σ bonds in the bisected conformation: tricyclopropylmethyl (pKR+ −2.3, more stable than trityl) > dicyclopropyl > cyclopropylmethyl.
E2-21.
Arrange 1–3 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 1 > 2 > 3
Methyl groups on the cyclopropane ring increase its donor strength (+I and hyperconjugation).
E2-23.
Arrange 1–3 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 2 > 1 > 3
2 and 1 are tertiary, 3 secondary. Ring cation 2 beats 1 because a five-membered ring prefers sp2 carbon (I-strain: 1-methylcyclopentyl solvolyses ≈ 40× faster than t-butyl).
E2-24.
Arrange 1–3 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 3 > 2 > 1
An α-oxygen lone pair gives an oxocarbenium ion (+M ≫ hyperconjugation); the tertiary α-alkoxy ion also has two methyl groups.
E2-25.
Arrange 1–3 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 3 > 2 > 1
An α-nitrogen lone pair gives an iminium ion; the more alkylated carbon (3) is better still. All are far more stable than the simple secondary alkyl cation 1.
E2-26.
Arrange 1–4 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 4 > 2 > 3 > 1
Two nitrogen lone pairs (an amidinium-type ion, 4) > two oxygens (2) > one oxygen (3). Ion 1 would be best electronically (three oxygens) but it sits at a bridgehead of a rigid cage and cannot become planar, so the empty p orbital cannot overlap with the oxygen lone pairs: it is the least stable.
E2-27.
Arrange 1–4 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 4 > 2 > 3 > 1
N is a better π donor than O: N,N (4) > N,O (2) > O,O (3); the cage cation 1 is non-planar at the bridgehead and cannot be stabilised by resonance.
E2-28.
Arrange 1–4 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 3 > 2 > 1 > 4
Tropylium (aromatic 6π) is the most stable; cyclopropylmethyl (bisected σ-donation, ‘dancing resonance’) > benzyl (resonance) > tert-butyl (hyperconjugation only) by the usual JEE convention that resonance ≫ hyperconjugation. Note: measured gas-phase hydride affinities put t-Bu+ (≈ 231 kcal mol−1) slightly below benzyl (≈ 238), i.e. t-Bu+ is the more stable in the gas phase; in solution the conventional order is the experimentally expected one for solvolysis.
E2-29.
Arrange 1–3 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 3 > 1 > 2
3 is tertiary; 1 is secondary (and will rearrange by a methyl shift to a tertiary ion); 2 is the primary neopentyl cation.
E2-30.
Arrange 1–3 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 3 > 1 > 2
Tertiary > secondary > primary.
E2-31.
Arrange 1–3 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 1 > 3 > 2
1 is allylic (resonance); 3 is a simple secondary cation; 2, the cyclopentadienyl cation, is antiaromatic (4π) and the least stable.
E2-32.
Arrange 1–3 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 1 > 3 > 2
Tropylium (aromatic, 6π) > cyclohex-2-enyl (allylic) > cyclopentadienyl (antiaromatic).
E2-35.
Arrange 1–3 in decreasing stability.
Answer: 1 > 2 > 3
1 is tertiary (ring fusion); 2 and 3 are secondary, and 2 has the branched ring-fusion carbon adjacent to C+ (more hyperconjugation) while 3 does not.
E2-91.
Which allylic carbocation is the most stable? (a) CH3–CH=CH–CH2+, (b) CH3–CH=CH–CH+–CH3, (c) CH3–CH=CH–C+(CH3)2, (d) all have the same stability.
Answer: (c)
Each is an allyl cation delocalised over two carbons, but the alkyl groups at the termini differ: (a) has a primary terminus, (b) a secondary, (c) a tertiary terminus. Charge is shared by both termini, so the more substituted ion (c) is the most stable. (d) is wrong: the alkyl substitution differs.
E2-93.
Which of the following carbocations is the most stable? (a) tricyclopropylmethyl, (b) benzyl, (c) tropylium (cycloheptatrienyl), (d) isopropyl.
Answer: (c)
Tropylium is aromatic (6π, planar, charge shared by seven carbons; pKR+ +4.7): the order is tropylium > tricyclopropylmethyl > benzyl > isopropyl.

Items from your exercise that need confirmation

I could not read these structures reliably from the images, so I have not answered them. Please tell me (or send a clearer image of) the exact substituents: Q4 (positions of the two methyl groups on each cyclohexyl cation), Q18 and Q19 (the ring substituents on the benzyl cations are not visible), Q22 (the polyspiro cyclopropane/cyclobutane cations: the geometry of the spiro rings relative to the cationic centre decides whether cyclopropyl donation can operate), Q33 (ring positions of the methyl groups) and Q34 (which carbons of the oxygen heterocycles carry the double bonds).

Part 5B Worked Solutions: the Supplied ‘Electronic Displacement Effects’ Carbocation Problems (redrawn)

These are the carbocation-stability items from the ‘Exercise O-II’ set you supplied (Q8–Q16 of that exercise). Structures are redrawn and the reasoning is new. Orders are decreasing stability unless the question says otherwise, using JEE-Advanced conventions; where the textbook key conflicts with measured data it is flagged. The carbanion and radical items from the same pages (Q17–Q20) are answered in the carbanion and free-radical chapters, and the aromaticity, bond-length and resonance-energy items belong with those topics.

E3-8.
Select the least stable cation.
Answer: (A)
All four are primary. Each larger alkyl group is a better +I donor and more polarisable, so ethyl, with the smallest substituent, is the least stable. (Counting α-C–H bonds alone would favour ethyl, which is why this is a ‘+I/polarisability’ answer, not a hyperconjugation one.)
E3-9(i).
Arrange in decreasing stability.
Answer: c > b > a
Tertiary > secondary > primary.
E3-9(ii).
Arrange in decreasing stability.
Answer: c > b > a
c is tertiary; a and b are secondary, and b carries an extra adjacent methyl-bearing carbon (more α-C–C/C–H hyperconjugation).
E3-9(iv).
Arrange the cycloalkyl cations in decreasing stability.
Answer: d > c > b > a (textbook key)
Textbook key: angle strain at the sp2 centre (60° in cyclopropyl, 90° in cyclobutyl) destabilises the small rings. Conflict with data: solvolysis rates (I-strain) make cyclopentyl faster than cyclohexyl, and cyclobutyl is stabilised by non-classical bridging, so the experimental order is closer to c > d > b > a. If a question forces one answer, use the key; know the data.
E3-9(v).
Arrange in decreasing stability.
Answer: c > b > a
All three groups are −I; the strength of the effect follows electronegativity, F ≫ Cl > Br, so CBr3 destabilises least.
E3-9(vii).
Arrange in decreasing stability.
Answer: c > b > a
The empty orbital sits on sp (50% s) or sp2 (33% s) carbon: the more s-character, the more tightly held the electrons and the less stable the cation. Ethyl uses a p orbital.
E3-9(viii).
Arrange the aryl cations in decreasing stability.
Answer: c > a > d > b
The empty sp2 orbital lies in the ring plane, orthogonal to the π system, so there is no resonance: only the inductive effect operates. CH3 is +I; Cl is −I and NO2 is more strongly −I.
E3-9(ix).
Arrange the benzyl cations in decreasing stability.
Answer: b > c > a
p-OMe donates by +M (oxocarbenium contributor); NO2 withdraws by −M and −I.
E3-9(x).
Arrange the hydroxybenzyl cations in decreasing stability.
Answer: c > a > b
Ortho and para OH can place the positive charge on oxygen (+M); meta cannot, and there OH is only −I. Para is better than ortho by the usual key (ortho: the −I effect is stronger at short distance and the oxygen lone pair is nearer the charge).
E3-9(xi).
Arrange the methylbenzyl cations in decreasing stability.
Answer: c > a > b
Ortho and para CH3 hyperconjugate with the delocalised charge; meta cannot. Textbook key puts ortho first (closer +I and hyperconjugation); steric effects can reverse this in real systems.
E3-9(xii).
Arrange the p-alkylbenzyl cations in decreasing stability.
Answer: a > b > c > d
Baker–Nathan order: the number of hyperconjugating α-C–H bonds is 3, 2, 1, 0. (Pure inductive donation would give the opposite order.)
E3-9(xiii).
Arrange in decreasing stability.
Answer: b > a > c > d
Trityl (three-ring delocalisation) > tertiary alkyl > primary alkyl > phenyl cation (no resonance, charge in an sp2 orbital).
E3-9(xv).
Arrange in decreasing stability.
Answer: a > c > b
Cyclopropylmethyl is stabilised by bent-bond donation (σ → p overlap in the bisected conformation); cyclopentyl is secondary; cyclobutylmethyl is an ordinary primary cation.
E3-9(xvi).
Arrange in decreasing stability.
Answer: b > c > a
Tropylium is aromatic (6π); cyclopent-2-enyl is allylic; cyclopentadienyl is antiaromatic (4π) and the least stable of all.
E3-10.
Which statements are correct? (I) CH3OCH2+ is more stable than CH3CH2+. (II) (CH3)2CH+ is more stable than CH3CH2CH2+. (III) CH2=CH–CH2+ is more stable than CH3CH2CH2+. (IV) CH2=CH+ is more stable than CH3CH2+. (A) I, II (B) III, IV (C) I, II, III (D) II, III, IV
Answer: (C)
I: α-oxygen lone pair gives an oxocarbenium ion. II: secondary > primary. III: allyl resonance. IV is false: the vinyl cation has an sp-hybridised cationic carbon, which is less stable than ethyl.
E3-11a/b.
Which ion is more stable? (a) C6H5CH2+ or CH2=CH–CH2+; (b) CH3CH2+ or CH2=CH+.
Answer: (a) benzyl; (b) ethyl
(a) Benzyl delocalises the charge over four carbons (seven contributors incl. ring), allyl over two. (b) The vinyl cation is sp-hybridised and the empty p orbital has no hyperconjugating partners except one C–H.
E3-13.
Which is the most stable? (A) Ph3C+ (B) (CH3)3C+ (C) (CH3)2CH+ (D) CH2=CH–CH2+
Answer: (A)
Trityl: charge is delocalised over three rings (ten carbons’ worth of contributors); pKR+ = −6.6 compared with about −15 for t-butyl.
E3-14.
Increasing order of stability of (a) p-CH3O–C6H4CH2+ (b) C6H5CH2+ (c) p-CH3–C6H4CH2+ (d) CH3CH2+.
Answer: d < b < c < a → (A)
Ethyl (no resonance) < benzyl < p-methylbenzyl (hyperconjugation) < p-methoxybenzyl (+M).
E3-15.
Correct order of stability: (1) p-HO– (2) p-H2N– (3) p-CH3– (4) p-(CH3)3C– benzyl cation.
Answer: 2 > 1 > 3 > 4 → (D)
NH2 is a stronger +M donor than OH (σ+ −1.3 vs −0.92); CH3 has three α-C–H bonds, t-Bu none.
E3-16.
Increasing order of stability: (I) p-methylbenzyl, (II) p-nitrobenzyl, (III) 3,5-diisopropyl-4-nitrobenzyl cation.
Answer: II < III < I → (B)
Steric inhibition of resonance: the two flanking isopropyl groups twist the nitro group out of the ring plane, so it loses its −M effect and only −I remains. III is therefore less destabilised than II (full −M and −I), but still less stable than the methyl-substituted I.

Part 5C Worked Solutions: Supplied ‘How Many’ Counting Problems (redrawn)

Counting problems need every item judged correctly, so the reasoning for each item is given. The structures are redrawn from your images; where a drawing was ambiguous I state the reading I used, because a different reading can change the count. Items marked ◊ are the ones to double-check against your original.

C-7.
How many of these cations are more stable than the benzyl cation?
Answer: 3 (p-OCH3, p-OH, p-NH2)
Only +M donors in the ortho/para position beat hydrogen: p-OMe, p-OH and p-NH2 (σ+ −0.78, −0.92, −1.3). o-NO2 and m-NO2 are strongly −I (−M too in the ortho case). m-OMe and m-F act only by −I, because no resonance contributor puts charge on the meta carbon. o-Cl is −I and its +M is weak (σ+p Cl = +0.11, i.e. slightly destabilising), so it is below benzyl.
C-11a.
Among the pairs, how many have (i) more reactive than (ii) towards AgNO3? (Reactivity = ease of ionising C–X, i.e. stability of the carbocation formed; SN1 path.)
Answer: 3 (B, D and E)
A: both give an oxocarbenium ion; in my reading (ii) is also allylic, so (ii) is more reactive (not counted). If (ii) is an isolated or enol-ether double bond the pair would count, so check the position of the double bond. B: (i) loses Br− to give the pyrylium ion, aromatic (6π, O lone pair + two C=C); (ii) would give the antiaromatic cyclopentadienyl cation. (i) ≫ (ii): counts. C: reading (i) as 5-iodocyclopenta-1,3-diene, ionisation gives the antiaromatic cyclopentadienyl cation, much worse than a plain secondary cyclopentyl cation, so (i) is less reactive (not counted). If (i) were 3-iodocyclopentene (allylic) it would count. D: (i) gives the aromatic tropylium ion; (ii) the antiaromatic cyclopentadienyl cation: counts. E: (i) is a secondary 2-chloronorbornane (ionises, with σ-participation); (ii) is a bridgehead chloride, whose cation cannot become planar: counts.
C-12a.
How many of the following are more stable than the isopropyl cation, owing to +R together with −I effects?
Answer: 3 (B, C and J)
A +R group must be bonded directly to C+ with a free lone pair. B is an oxocarbenium ion and C and J are iminium ions: all three are far more stable than a secondary alkyl cation. D: the nitrogen lone pair is tied up in the N→O bond, so there is no +R and a strong −I (N+–O−). A, E, H and I have the heteroatom or halogen one or more carbons away from C+: only −I operates, which destabilises. F: propargyl is resonance-stabilised but the sp carbon is −I, and it is less stable than secondary alkyl (gas-phase hydride affinity higher than i-Pr+). G: α-carbonyl cation, destabilised by −I and −M.
C-11b.
Species: quinuclidine, cyclooctatetraene, naphthalene, cyclopropenyl cation, tropylium ion, propene, 1,3-butadiene. x = number in which resonance takes place; y = number in which every C–C bond length is equal. Find (x² + y² + 1)/(x + y + 1).
Answer: x = 4, y = 2, value = 21/7 = 3
Resonance (π delocalisation) occurs in naphthalene, the cyclopropenyl cation, tropylium and 1,3-butadiene: x = 4. Quinuclidine has no π system; cyclooctatetraene is tub-shaped, so its double bonds do not conjugate (alternating bond lengths); propene only has hyperconjugation. All C–C bonds are equal only in the cyclopropenyl and tropylium cations (complete delocalisation round a symmetric ring): y = 2. Naphthalene (1.36/1.42 Å) and butadiene have unequal bonds; in quinuclidine C2–C3 and C3–C4 are not symmetry-equivalent. (16 + 4 + 1)/(4 + 2 + 1) = 3.
C-12b.
How many of the following cations are more stable than the benzyl cation?
Answer: 3 (iii, iv, vi)
iii: tricyclopropylmethyl (pKR+ −2.3) is more stable than benzyl. iv: α-methoxybenzyl is both benzylic and an oxocarbenium ion. vi: an alkyl-substituted cyclopropenyl cation is aromatic (2π, pKR+ about +10). i: phenyl cation has its empty orbital in the ring plane, no resonance. ii: allyl is less stabilised than benzyl. v: the norbornyl cation at C7 (or at a bridgehead) is held non-planar and cannot delocalise. vii: ordinary primary cation. viii: antiaromatic. ix: m-OMe is only −I.
C-15.
How many of the given cations are more stable than the ethyl cation?
Answer: 3 (i, ii, iii)
i: secondary > primary. ii: resonance. iii: bent-bond donation from the cyclopropane ring. iv: methyl cation is less stable than ethyl (no hyperconjugation). v and vi: the −I effect of Cl and NO2 destabilises the classical ion. (Real β-chloroalkyl cations are in fact bridged chloronium ions, which are lower in energy than a classical ethyl cation; the exam-level answer treats v as destabilised.)
C-23.
How many carbocations undergo rearrangement?
Answer: 7 (i, iii, vii, ix, x, xi, xii)
A cation rearranges only if a 1,2-shift gives a more stable ion. i 2,2-dimethylcyclohexyl (2°) → methyl shift → tertiary. iii cyclopentylmethyl (1°) → hydride shift to 1-methylcyclopentyl (3°), or ring expansion to cyclohexyl. vii cyclopropylcarbinyl-type: ring expansion of the cyclopropane to a cyclobutyl ring gives a tertiary ion. ix pinacol-type: ring-carbon migration to the cationic carbon expands the ring and gives a protonated ketone (2,2-dimethylcycloheptanone). x this is an ipso arenium ion with a spiro carbon: a 1,2 alkyl shift restores the aromatic ring (dienone–phenol type). xi neopentyl → methyl shift → tert-amyl. xii Ph2CH–C+Me2 → hydride shift → Ph2C+–CHMe2 (diphenylmethyl-type, more stable). No rearrangement: ii cycloheptyl (a hydride shift gives the same type of ion), iv an α-hydroxy carbenium ion is already stabilised by oxygen, and the shift would lose that, v benzyl, vi vinyl, viii allyl (resonance, not rearrangement).

Part 5D Worked Solutions: More Supplied Counting Problems (heterolysis, statements, rearrangement, AgNO3)

Structures are redrawn from your images. Items marked ◊ were hard to read; the reading I used is stated, and a different reading can change the count. Conventions as before: the JEE key ranks resonance above hyperconjugation, so benzyl is taken as more stable than t-butyl even though gas-phase hydride affinities say otherwise.

D-27.
For how many compounds is the heterolytic C–Cl bond energy less than that of (CH3)3C–Cl? (A lower heterolysis energy means a more stable cation is formed than t-Bu+.)
Answer: 4 (I, II, IV, V)
I gives the acylium ion CH3C≡O+, stabilised by oxygen lone-pair donation: counts (conventional key). II benzyl (resonance over the ring): counts. IV 3-chlorocyclopropene gives the aromatic cyclopropenyl cation: counts. V cyclopropylmethyl cation (bent-bond donation, more stable than benzyl): counts. III and VII: aryl and vinyl cations (sp2/sp, no resonance, C–Cl also strengthened by p–π overlap): no. VIII primary and IX secondary: less stable than tertiary. VI allyl: a primary cation with two resonance forms, ranked below the tertiary cation by the usual key (gas-phase hydride affinity agrees: allyl is less stable than t-Bu+). If your source ranks allyl above tertiary the count would be 5.
D-38.
Find the number of correct statements.
Answer: 5 (i, ii, iii, iv, vi correct; v is wrong)
(i) Cyclopentadienyl cation is antiaromatic (4π); cyclopropenyl is aromatic (2π): the statement is correct. (ii) Ethyl is less stable than methoxymethyl (oxocarbenium, +M): correct. (iii) −CH2NO2 is delocalised onto oxygen (nitronate), much better than benzyl anion: correct. (iv) p-CH3 donates, CCl3 withdraws (−I): p-methylbenzyl > benzyl > p-CCl3-benzyl: correct. (v) Benzyl anion is delocalised into the ring and is much more stable than cyclopropylmethyl anion, which only has a weak s-character effect: the correct order is benzyl > cyclopropylmethyl > ethyl, so the statement is wrong. (vi) Singlet carbene stability follows π-donation from halogen lone pairs into the empty p orbital, best for 2p–2p overlap with F, then Cl, Br, I: CF2 > CCl2 > CBr2 > CI2: correct.
D-19 / D-21b.
How many of these carbocations can undergo rearrangement? (The same set appears twice in your pages.)
Answer: 4 (d, f, i, k)
d cyclohexylmethyl (1°): hydride shift to 1-methylcyclohexyl (3°) or ring expansion to cycloheptyl. f 3-methyl-2-norbornyl (2°): hydride shift from the methyl-bearing carbon gives the tertiary 2-methyl-2-norbornyl ion. i pinacol-type (CH3)2C+–C(OH)(CH3)–: a methyl shift gives a protonated ketone. k the β-alkoxy primary cation ⁺CH2CH2OR: a 1,2-hydride shift gives the oxocarbenium ion CH3CH+OR, far more stable. No rearrangement: a tertiary (3-methyl-3-pentyl, as I read it); b ethyl (the only shift is degenerate); c tertiary; e benzyl; g tertiary 2-methylnorbornyl (a shift would only give another tertiary or a less stable ion); h allylic; j cyclohexyl (the 1,2-H shift is degenerate; ring contraction to methylcyclopentyl is only seen in superacid, so it is not counted at this level). ◊ If a is really a secondary cation next to a quaternary carbon, it would rearrange and the count becomes 5.
D-21a.
How many of the following give a white precipitate with aqueous AgNO3? (AgCl forms only if the C–Cl bond ionises readily, i.e. the cation is very stable.)
Answer: 4 (1, 6, 7, 8)
1 3-chlorocyclopropene → aromatic cyclopropenyl cation. 6 7-chlorocycloheptatriene → tropylium chloride (an ionic salt, immediate AgCl). 7 1-chlorocyclopentanol: an α-chloro alcohol loses Cl− to give the protonated ketone (oxocarbenium), then cyclopentanone. 8 dicyclopropylmethyl chloride: the cation is stabilised by two cyclopropyl groups. 2 cyclopropyl chloride: the cyclopropyl cation is strained and unstable (ionisation and ring-opening are concerted and slow). 3, 4 I read these as 5-chlorocyclopenta-1,3-dienes: loss of Cl− would give the antiaromatic cyclopentadienyl cation, so no precipitate. 5 I read this as a chloromethyl group on a saturated ring position, an ordinary primary chloride: no precipitate. ◊ Please check items 3–5 against your page: if any of them is allylic (for example 3-chlorocyclopentene) it would give a precipitate.

Part 5E Your ‘Stability of Carbocation’ Notes (cation.pdf): everything added, redrawn and checked

This part reproduces the content of the 11-page handwritten note you supplied: the factor list, the worked orders 1–12, the pKR+ ladder, the gas-phase hydride-affinity table, the tabulated pK values, σ-bond resonance and the non-classical ions, and the aryl-cation substituent series. Structures are redrawn; numerical values are transcribed from your pages (they are literature values quoted in the note, not independently re-measured here). Where something in the note disagrees with another part of the same note, or with the data it quotes, the disagreement is marked ⚑ Check and the reasoning is given, so you can decide which to use in an exam.

5E.1 The factor list

Stabilising factorRule from the noteComment
+R / +Mstability ∝ +R/+Mlone-pair or π donation into the empty p orbital; the strongest effect (oxocarbenium, iminium, arylmethyl with p-OMe/NR2)
+H (hyperconjugation)∝ number of α C–H (and C–C) bondscounted on the carbon next to C+; 9α > 6α > 4α in example 3
+I∝ electron release by alkylmatters when hyperconjugation is absent or equal
−I, −H, −Mstability ∝ 1/(−I), 1/(−H), 1/(−M)withdrawing groups, loss of hyperconjugating bonds, and acceptors destabilise

The note adds two measured quantities: the gas-phase hydride affinity (HIA; lower = more stable cation) and the solution pKR+ (higher = more stable cation). They are separate observables and, as the note's own data show, do not always give the same order.

5E.2 Worked orders 1–12 (redrawn)

1. Longer conjugation: a < b < c (allyl < pentadienyl < heptatrienyl); more resonance contributors spread the charge over more carbons.
2. a < b. The pentadienyl cation a has a sextet on carbon; in b oxygen gives a lone pair so every atom has an octet (oxocarbenium).
3. 9α > 6α > 4α, i.e. hyperconjugation by α C–H bond count (H > I). ⚑ Check: as drawn (second and third), the counts follow the note; the middle cation is tertiary and the last secondary, so the order is also tertiary > … secondary, which agrees.
4. CH3+ < CD3+ < CT3+. The isotopes sit on C+, so no C–X bond is hyperconjugating: only the +I order T > D > H is left.
5. (CH3)3C+ > (CD3)3C+ > (CT3)3C+. Now the labelled groups are β to the charge: hyperconjugation dominates, and C–H (weakest, highest zero-point energy) donates best. The note summarises: +I order CT3 > CD3 > CH3; hyperconjugation (+H) order CH3 > CD3 > CT3 (BDE C–T > C–D > C–H); the +H effect wins.
6. As drawn in the note: a > b (phenyl cation > cyclohexyl cation).
⚑ Check, item 6. This inequality is the wrong way round on the note's own data: the hydride affinity table (5E.4) gives phenyl 294 and a secondary cation (isopropyl) 249 kcal/mol; a secondary cyclohexyl cation is therefore far more stable than phenyl, whose empty orbital is an sp2 σ orbital in the ring plane with no resonance. I recommend recording: cyclohexyl > phenyl. If your source key says otherwise, treat it as a misprint.
7. a < b < c: phenyl cation < diphenylmethyl < trityl (each phenyl delocalises the charge).
8. a < c < b: primary < secondary < tertiary.
9. a > b > c: the more s-character in the carbon bearing the empty orbital (sp3-like p, sp2, sp), the less stable the cation.
10. c > a > b. c is a cyclohexadienyl (pentadienyl-type, two C=C) cation; a and b are allylic secondary; a has a methyl-bearing carbon next to the cationic carbon (extra hyperconjugation), b only a remote one. ◊ Positions of the methyl and the ring double bonds are my reading of the drawing.
11. a < b as printed in the note (cyclic oxocarbenium: b has the + next to O).
⚑ Check, item 11. In the second structure the cation sits next to the ring oxygen only if the positive charge is on C2 (drawn at the position adjacent to O). That is the oxocarbenium ion, and it is more stable than the tertiary 1-methylcyclohexyl cation, which agrees with the note. If the cation were on C3 (β to O) the −I effect would make it less stable than the tertiary ion; item 12 shows exactly that difference.
12. a > b > c: oxygen donates its lone pair when the cation is α (C2); at C3 and C4 only the −I effect operates, strongest at C3 (nearer to O).

5E.3 ‘Important order’: the pKR+ ladder

pKR+ is defined from the equilibrium R+ + H2O ⇌ ROH + H+ by pKR+ = log([R+]/[ROH]) + HR, where HR is the acidity function that plays the role of pH in strong acid. A cation with a larger pKR+ persists at a more acidic medium, i.e. is more stable. (Your note writes the equilibrium as H+ + ROH ⇌ R+ + H2O; that is the same reaction read in the cation-forming direction, and the formula above is the standard one.)

Aromatic cations first: tricyclopropylcyclopropenyl > trimethylcyclopropenyl > tropylium > triphenylcyclopropenyl.
…then tricyclopropylmethyl > (parent cyclopropenyl, value as printed) > Ph3C+ > Ph2CH+ > PhCH(CH3)+ > (CH3)3C+ > PhCH2+.
…then allyl > isopropyl > ethyl (−29.9) > methyl > vinyl > ethynyl (−40.2).
⚑ Check (values). (1) Your ladder gives t-Bu+ = −16.4, but the Carey–Sundberg table on page 6 of the same note gives −15.5 (and McManus's page says ‘estimate −15.5’ in FSO3H–SbF5); I would use −15.5. (2) The tricyclopropylcyclopropenyl cation is +9.7 on the ladder and in the Carey table, but ‘7.2’ on page 5. (3) Tropylium is +4.7 on the ladder and in Carey, ‘4.2’ on page 5. (4) The ladder puts the parent cyclopropenyl cation at −5.5; I cannot confirm this value from the tables you supplied, so it is marked ◊. Important consequence: on this ladder t-butyl (−16.4/−15.5) is above benzyl (≈ −20), and 2-phenyl-2-propyl (cumyl, −12.3) is above both. So on your source's data, t-Bu+ is more stable than the benzyl cation, not less. Earlier parts of this book use the usual ‘resonance > hyperconjugation’ coaching convention for benzyl vs t-Bu in some answers and flag it; with this note as your source, use t-Bu+ > benzyl. This changes the count in D-27 (below).

5E.6 Examples from the note (March / Carey sets): where they appear in this book

The nine orders printed on your page 3 under ‘Source – Jerry March’ are the same problems as your Exercise 2 and are answered, with reasons, in Part 5A. Two points need to be stated here.

If the examiner's key matches the page, it is the key's choice, not the data's.

Heptaphenyltropylium (+7) is more stable than tropylium (+4.7/4.2): phenyl groups add some conjugation and steric protection. Tris(p-anisyl)cyclopropenyl (+6.5) > triphenylcyclopropenyl (+3.1): p-OMe donates.
Amino-substituted cyclopropenyl cations: the stronger the donor, the larger the pKR+.
⚑ Check. (a) +7.2 for tricyclopropylcyclopropenyl contradicts +9.7 elsewhere (use +9.7, which is the Carey–Sundberg value). (b) +9.36 is, in Carey–Sundberg, the value for the triarylmethyl cation with three p-dimethylamino groups (crystal-violet type), not for the cyclopropenyl analogue; confirm which structure your source means before using the number. The trend (donors raise pK) is not in doubt.
Benzotropylium (+1.7, a benzo-fused seven-membered ring cation), tris(p-anisyl)methyl, tris(p-tolyl)methyl, trityl and diphenylmethyl: stability follows the donor strength of the para groups.

5E.8 Pentavalent carbonium ions and σ-bond resonance

Carbonium ions (five-coordinate carbon): CH5+ (methanonium) and C2H7+ (ethanonium) contain a three-centre two-electron (3c–2e) C···H···C or C···H···H unit: the bonding pair of a C–H σ bond is shared by three atoms. They are observed in the gas phase and in superacid (CH5+ is a true, fluxional species); in ordinary solution chemistry they appear as transition states or short-lived intermediates (your note writes ‘T.S. or true intermediate’). Do not confuse them with carbenium ions (three-coordinate R3C+), which are the ions of all the other parts.

σ-bond resonance (‘dancing resonance’) in the cyclopropylmethyl cation: the C–C σ bonds of cyclopropane are bent and strained, and their electrons are close in energy to a π bond (cyclopropane behaves electronically as a very weak π-donor). In the bisected conformation the empty p orbital lies parallel to the plane of the ring bonds, so a ring σ bond can overlap with it. The cation is then a hybrid of cyclopropylcarbinyl ⇌ homoallyl (CH2=CH–CH2–CH2+) contributors with partial δ+ on the ring carbons, the three ‘R.H.’ charges drawn in the note. Your note says the effect is ‘even stronger than +H’: that is correct as a statement of stabilisation (cyclopropylmethyl > benzyl on most measures); the description of the C–C bond as ‘weaker than the π bond of an alkene’ is a simplification: it is strained, and its electrons are much easier to donate than an ordinary C–C σ bond, which is the reason it works.

Order from the note: cyclopropylmethyl < 2-methyl-cyclopropylmethyl < 2,3-dimethyl-cyclopropylmethyl (methyl groups on the ring improve the donor); p-cyclopropylbenzyl > p-cyclobutylbenzyl (cyclopropyl donates by σ-resonance, cyclobutyl does not). And p-cyclopropylbenzyl > 3,5-dimethyl-4-cyclopropylbenzyl: the two methyl groups ortho to the cyclopropyl group force the ring out of the bisected arrangement, so the donation is lost (steric inhibition of resonance).

a > b (σ-resonance); a > c (steric inhibition of resonance by the flanking methyls).
Tropylium (4.7) < heptaphenyltropylium (7): see 5E.7. The cation has seven equivalent resonance contributors (aromatic, 6π over 7 carbons).

5E.9 Non-classical cations from the note

  • Phenonium ion: β-phenylethyl cation C6H5CH2CH2+ is bridged by the ring π electrons to give a spiro[2.5]octadienyl (phenonium) cation, with the starred label carbon becoming equivalent to its partner by the shift; the ring is a σ/π donor through its ipso carbon (sketch in your note: ring in dotted outline bonded to both CH2 carbons).
  • 7-Norbornenyl / nortricyclyl system: the π bond of norbornene participates with a developing cation at C7, giving a delocalised three-centre σ/π ion; the note draws the two limiting structures and the hybrid with dotted partial bonds.
  • 2-Norbornyl cation (page 8): classical ion ⇌ σ-bridged (non-classical) ion, drawn with the C1–C6 bond delocalised to C2 (see Part 4 for the full discussion and the evidence).
  • 1-Adamantyl cation: a bridgehead tertiary cation; it cannot flatten, but is stabilised by hyperconjugation from the three β C–C bonds and is observable in superacid; it solvolyses much slower than t-butyl in comparable media, which is why it is the usual example of a ‘bridgehead’ cation.
Left to right: the phenonium ion drawn as its spiro cyclohexadienyl (arenium) contributor, the 1-adamantyl cation, and a classical 7-norbornyl cation. ◊ Bridged ions are hybrids that a single line-bond structure cannot draw faithfully (see Part 4).

5E.10 Aryl-cation substituent series (pages 10 and 11)

These series are for aryl cations (empty orbital on a ring carbon); the note uses the substituent effects as a guide to the order. Remember what the empty orbital is: an sp2 σ orbital in the ring plane, orthogonal to the π system, so the π-donor effect (+M) cannot operate by direct conjugation; the orders below therefore mix inductive effects with the textbook ‘conjugation-type’ rules the note uses. Note the three groups of series: +I alkyl (a < b < c < d < e), halogens (distance and electronegativity), and donors/acceptors (OH, NH2, OCH3, NO2, CCl3).

a < b < c < d < e: stability rises with the +I strength of the alkyl group (Me < Et < i-Pr < t-Bu).
a > d > c > b: the −I effect is strongest for F, then Cl, then Br; all are below the unsubstituted ion.
a > d > c > b: −I falls with distance, so the para ion is least destabilised and the ortho the most. (Your page prints the last symbol as ‘d’; it should read ‘b’, a typo.)
a > c > b > d as printed (m > o > p).
⚑ Check, nitro series. For chlorine the note uses a pure distance order (p > m > o); for NO2 it puts p-NO2 below o-NO2 (treating the −M effect as the extra factor at the para position). If only the in-plane σ cation is considered, −M cannot act and the distance (−I) order p > m > o, as for Cl, would be expected. The note's order is the one to use if your exam source is this note; keep in mind that the two series follow different rules.
d > b > a > c (OH: ortho −I,+M; meta −I only; para +M). The same series is given for NH2 (d > b > a > c) and for OCH3 (d > b > a > c).
NH2: d > b > a > c.
OCH3: d > b > a > c.
b > c > d > a: the para alkyl group donates by hyperconjugation, in proportion to its α C–H count (3, 2, 1), all better than hydrogen (Baker–Nathan type order).
CCl3: a > c > d > b as printed (ortho worst: −I plus loss of hyperconjugation; meta > para as printed).
Phenyl cation < CH2+–OCH3 (oxocarbenium; ≈ 294 vs far lower HIA).

5E.11 Carbanion stability (the note ends here)

The last page begins the next topic: carbanion stability ∝ −M, −H (loss of hyperconjugation destabilises less than donating groups destabilise a carbanion; here the note means electron-withdrawing groups), −I, and ∝ 1/(+I), 1/(+H), 1/(+M): the exact mirror of the carbocation list. The carbanion chapter, still to be written, will cover this fully; I have not drawn conclusions from the single page you supplied.

5E.12 Effect on the earlier answer D-27

D-27 (heterolytic C–Cl bond energy less than that of t-BuCl). I answered 4 (acetyl chloride, benzyl, 3-chlorocyclopropene, cyclopropylmethyl) using the coaching convention ‘benzyl > tertiary’. With the data of your note (pKR+: t-Bu −16.4/−15.5, benzyl ≈ −20; HIA: t-Bu 231.9, benzyl 238) the benzyl cation is less stable than t-Bu+, so benzyl chloride does not count, and the answer becomes 3 (acetyl chloride [acylium, if counted], 3-chlorocyclopropene, cyclopropylmethyl chloride). Which of 3 or 4 your source wants depends on whether it follows the data or the convention; on the data of this note use 3. The same caveat applies to any earlier answer that ranks benzyl above tert-butyl (Part 5A, Q28 uses t-Bu last; its position is already flagged there).

Part 7 Carbocation Rearrangements — Counting Problems (opening section)

Counting problems test whether you can recognise a rearrangement before drawing any mechanism. Rules used (JEE-Advanced level): a carbocation rearranges by a 1,2-H, 1,2-alkyl, 1,2-aryl or ring-bond shift only if the new cation is more stable (more substituted, conjugated, or less strained) or the new ion is trapped irreversibly; shifts to an equally stable cation (secondary → secondary, tertiary → tertiary) are degenerate or unproductive and are not counted as ‘rearranging’; tertiary, benzylic and allylic cations do not rearrange to a less stable ion. Primary cations are usually not true intermediates: the shift is concerted with the departure of the leaving group, but for counting purposes such a shift is ‘a rearrangement’. The answers below were cross-checked with a small shift-enumeration program (every 1,2-shift of every cation was generated and the product classified) and by hand.

7.1 How many rearrange? How many ring-expand? How many shifts are possible?

R1.How many of the following carbocations (a–j) will undergo rearrangement by a 1,2-shift to give a more stable carbocation? (Integer answer)
R2.How many of the carbocations (a–h) can undergo ring expansion by a single 1,2-shift to a more stable cation (more substituted and/or less strained)? (Integer answer)
R3.The 3-methylbutan-2-yl cation, CH3–CH+–CH(CH3)2, can undergo different 1,2-shifts. (i) How many different carbocations (other than the starting ion itself) can be formed by one 1,2-shift of H or CH3? (ii) How many of these are more stable than the starting ion? Give (i), (ii).
R4.How many 1,2-shifts, at minimum, convert the primary 3,3-dimethylbutyl cation, (CH3)3C–CH2–CH2+, into the most stable carbocation that is reachable? (Integer answer; each hydride, alkyl or ring-bond shift counts one.)
R5.3,3-Dimethylbutan-2-ol is heated with conc. H3PO4 (E1). How many different alkenes (structural isomers, counting only constitutional isomers, no stereoisomers arise) can be formed from all the carbocations that are intermediates, including the rearranged one? (Integer answer)
R6.Each compound (a–h) is treated with NaNO2/HCl at 0–5 °C, then the solution is allowed to stand. How many of the compounds give a carbocation as an intermediate (free, or as a tight ion pair, formed by loss of N2)? (Integer answer)
R7.Each alcohol (a–h) is heated with conc. HBr. How many give the alkyl bromide (or major product) with a rearranged carbon skeleton or rearranged position of Br through a carbocation or a concerted shift? (Integer answer)
R8.Benzene is alkylated with each alkyl chloride (a–h) and AlCl3. How many give a product in which the carbon skeleton or the point of attachment of the alkyl group differs from the alkyl chloride used (a rearranged product as the major product)? (Integer answer)

Answers Part 3 — Leaving-Group Problems: Answers and Explanations

LG1.
Answer: D > C > B > A
Rate-limiting heterolysis of C–X. Bond strength (C–I 57 ≪ C–F 110 kcal mol−1), polarisability and conjugate-acid strength (HI −10, HBr −9, HCl −7, HF +3.2) all point the same way. Solvation of F− by hydrogen bonding is the strongest of the four but cannot make up for the C–F bond: t-BuF is usually considered inert to neutral solvolysis. The three heavier halides differ only by modest factors (a few-fold between I and Br; tens between Br and Cl) because the TS is highly ionic and the solvent levels the differences.
LG2.
Answer: A > B > C > D
Leaving-group quality follows conjugate-acid strength: CF3SO3H (≈ −14) ≫ TsOH (≈ −2.8) ≫ CH3CO2H (4.76) ≫ H2O (15.7). Triflates ionise ≈ 104–108 times faster than tosylates depending on substrate; acetates are practically inert under these conditions, and the alcohol D does not ionise at all (HO− is not a leaving group without protonation). A secondary substrate is chosen so that all three active derivatives react by borderline SN1/SN2 with solvent assistance; the order is the same for either.
LG3.
Answer: A > B > C > D
N2 is a vastly better leaving group than anything else (a very stable, non-basic molecule; ionisation of an alkyl diazonium is practically barrierless). H2O leaves from the protonated alcohol readily at 25 °C in acid (conjugate acid H3O+, pKa −1.7). NH3 is a much stronger base (NH4+ pKa 9.25), so the t-butylammonium ion is stable at room temperature and needs heat or very strong acid to lose NH3. Hydroxide in D is the worst: C–OH ionisation does not occur without protonation (D is therefore last, essentially inert).
LG4.
Answer: C > D > B > A
Carboxylate leaving groups follow the pKa of the parent acid: CF3CO2H 0.5 < p-O2NC6H4CO2H 3.44 < C6H5CO2H 4.20 < CH3CO2H 4.76. The same trend is the basis of the classical use of p-nitrobenzoates as ‘better’ leaving groups than acetates in mechanistic work on tertiary benzylic systems. Resonance donation within the ester (which strengthens the C–O bond) is similar for all four and cancels.
LG5.
Answer: A > B > C
In SNAr the rate-determining step is addition of the nucleophile to give the anionic Meisenheimer complex; C–X cleavage comes afterwards (fast). Fluorine, the most electronegative halogen, lowers the energy of the first TS by induction and polarises C–X; the C–F bond strength is irrelevant to the rate. Hence the ‘element effect’ F ≫ Cl ≳ Br > I, the reverse of SN2 – a decisive demonstration that leaving-group ability is mechanism-dependent. (Cl and Br are close; iodine is slowest.)
LG6.
Answer: D > C > B > A
The poorer the leaving group, the less C–LG bond cleavage has occurred in the E2 transition state; the TS becomes carbanion-like (E1cB-like) and the base removes the more acidic, more accessible hydrogen from the CH3 group, giving the Hofmann alkene. Literature trend for 2-pentyl X with ethoxide: I < Br (≈ 30 %) ≲ Cl (≈ 33 %) < F (≈ 70 %) < NMe3+ (≈ 95 % 1-pentene); I and Br differ only slightly. Here LG ability controls selectivity, not only rate.
LG7.
Answer: A > B > C > D > E
Y (recalled values): H2O 3.49 > HCO2H 2.05 > CF3CH2OH 1.15 > CH3OH −1.09 > C2H5OH −2.03. Ionising power combines hydrogen-bond donation to the departing chloride (high for water, HCO2H, fluorinated alcohols) with dielectric screening and low nucleophilicity. TFE is a poor nucleophile yet an excellent ionising medium, so SN1 reactions of secondary substrates are favoured there; a leaving group’s ‘ability’ is therefore also a property of the solvent.
LG8.
Answer: A > C > B
E2 needs the C–H and C–Br bonds anti-periplanar, which on a chair means both axial. In the cis isomer (A) the Br is axial (the locked t-Bu is equatorial), so reaction is fast. In the trans isomer (B) Br is equatorial, no anti-periplanar H exists, the ring would have to flip into the diaxial-t-Bu chair, and E2 is slow (substitution/E1 intrude). Bromocyclohexane (C) populates the axial conformer to a modest extent (≈ 30 %), so its rate lies between. The axial/equatorial labels refer to chairs, which these flat drawings cannot show; wedge/dash give the relative (cis/trans) configuration.
LG9.
Answer: A > B > C > D
The rate follows both the leaving-group stability (Cl−, pKa(HCl) −7; CH3CO2− 4.76; EtO− 16; NH2− 38) and the ability of the substituent to donate into C=O (N ≫ O > Cl). The tetrahedral intermediate expels the best leaving group; amides, with strong n(N) → π*(C=O) donation and a very poor LG, are the least reactive. Contrast with SN1/SN2 at sp3 carbon, where resonance donation is irrelevant.
LG10.
Answer: A > B > C
Trimethyloxonium (Meerwein) salts are among the strongest methylating agents; trimethylsulfonium is a weak methylating agent (it needs warming), and tetramethylammonium is inert. The leaving groups are Me2O, Me2S and Me3N. Basicity (pKaH of Me3N 9.8 ≫ Me2O ≈ −3.8, Me2S ≈ −6 to −7) explains why ammonium is last, but not why oxonium beats sulfonium: sulfur is the weaker base. Here the intrinsic C–X+ bond strength and the charge density at the cationic centre dominate – a clear failure of a pure pKa rule. (Experimental trend: O+ ≫ S+ ≫ N+.)
LG11.
Answer: A > B > C > D
Ag+ coordinates the halogen lone pair and ‘pulls’ the bromide off (halophilic assistance); the substrate then ionises. The ease of forming the cation is 3° ≫ 2° > 1° (t-Bu+ ≫ i-Pr+ ≫ n-Bu+); the n-butyl bromide reacts only slowly (a partial SN2-like displacement by solvent) and bromobenzene (an sp2 aryl cation would be needed) gives no precipitate. Same leaving group, different cation – the LG is only as good as the cation it can generate.
LG12.
Answer: A > B > C
β-Silicon effect: a C–Si σ bond is an excellent hyperconjugative donor (σC–Si is higher in energy than σC–C/σC–H) and stabilises a β cation by σ→p donation (a bridged, silicon-stabilised cation). The overlap is best when C–Si and C–OTs are anti-periplanar, which the trans isomer reaches in the diaxial chair (A: very large acceleration, ≈ 1012 in rigid models). The cis isomer (B) has them gauche (synclinal) only: still accelerated (≈ 104 in rigid models) but far less. Cyclohexyl tosylate (C) has no silicon. (Orders of magnitude quoted from Lambert’s work, recalled.)
LG13.
Answer: A > B > C > D
The aryl ring attacks the carbon carrying OTs from the rear, forming a bridged phenonium (spiro-cyclohexadienyl) ion; the rate rises with the electron-donating power of the para substituent (σ+: OMe −0.78, Me −0.31, H 0, NO2 +0.79). The p-nitro compound cannot use the ring and reacts by the slower, unassisted SN2-like route (ks). The ‘leaving group’ is identical (TsO−) in all four; the substituent changes how effectively it is displaced.
LG14.
Answer: A > B > C > D
The leaving group is the protonated oxygen (an alcohol or ether oxygen that becomes neutral on C–O cleavage), and the driving force is the release of ring strain: oxirane (≈ 27 kcal mol−1) and oxetane (≈ 25) are strained; oxolane (THF, ≈ 6) is slightly strained; oxane (THP, ≈ 0.5) is not. Epoxides react far faster than oxetanes despite similar strain energies because the TS gains from poorer C–O–C orbital overlap (bent bonds) in the three-membered ring; THF is cleaved only under more forcing conditions, THP hardly at all.
LG15.
Answer: A > B > C > D
The sulfonate anion is stabilised by electron-withdrawing substituents (lower pKa of ArSO3H), so the leaving-group ability follows the Hammett σ constants: NO2 (σp +0.78) > Br (+0.23) > CH3 (−0.17) > OCH3 (−0.27); ρ for the leaving group is positive and modest. Brosylates and nosylates are therefore used when tosylates are too unreactive; mesylates are comparable to tosylates.

Answer: (i) 2 (ii) 1
Shifts available: H from C-3 → 2-methylbut-2-yl, tertiary (more stable); CH3 from C-3 → regenerates a 3-methylbutan-2-yl cation (degenerate, not a new ion); H from the CH3 on C-2 → 3-methylbutyl, primary (less stable). Distinct new cations: tertiary and primary = 2; more stable: only the tertiary = 1. (Hydride shift is the productive path, reached through a three-centre transition state with σ(C–H) → p overlap.)
R4.
Answer: 2
Step 1: 1,2-hydride shift from the CH2 next to the quaternary carbon → 3,3-dimethylbut-2-yl (secondary). Step 2: 1,2-methyl shift from the quaternary carbon → 2,3-dimethylbut-2-yl (tertiary, the most stable ion in this manifold). A direct primary → tertiary shift is impossible because the tertiary centre is two bonds away. (The same cation is the one formed from 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol; see R5.)
R5.
Answer: 3
Unrearranged secondary cation (3,3-dimethylbut-2-yl): loses H+ only from CH3 (the other neighbour is quaternary) → 3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene (minor). After the 1,2-CH3 shift the tertiary 2,3-dimethylbut-2-yl cation loses H+ from the CH (→ 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene, tetrasubstituted, major) or from a CH3 (→ 2,3-dimethylbut-1-ene). Total 3; the Zaitsev (2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene) dominates.
